Q715.L1t: Word problems about fractions of a quantity are usually solved by turning the wording into an equation.
Q715.L2t: One-half of one-third of a pile is one-sixth of that pile, and the two piles were equal in size.
Q715.L3t: The brother's gift is one-sixth of a single pile, so John's remainder is the whole of both piles minus that one-sixth, which equals eleven-sixths of one pile.
Q715.L2f: Taking one-half of one-third of a quantity removes exactly one-fourth of it.
Q715.L3f: The 66 pins John had left equal one-sixth of his original total, so the total is six times the amount left.
Q715.L4f: John originally had three hundred ninety-six pins.

Q662.L1t: Geometric probability problems on a circle often reduce to comparing arc lengths with the full circumference.
Q662.L2t: A chord's length depends on the central angle it subtends, and chord length grows as that angle grows from 0 to 180 degrees.
Q662.L3t: A chord is shorter than the radius exactly when its central angle is under 60 degrees, so all three points must lie within a common arc of one-sixth of the circle.
Q662.L4t: The probability is one in twelve.
Q662.L2f: The chord length between two points on a circle depends only on the radius and not on how far apart the points are.
Q662.L3f: A chord equals the radius when its central angle is 45 degrees, so all three points must fit within an eighth of the circle and the favorable count is 2 times the square of one-eighth.
Q662.L4f: The probability is one in thirty-two.

Q729.L1t: Coordinate geometry lets you compute lengths and areas of polygons directly from vertex coordinates.
Q729.L2t: Opposite vertices of a square are the endpoints of a diagonal, and the distance formula gives the length between any two coordinate points.
Q729.L3t: The area of a square equals half the square of its diagonal, and here the diagonal's squared length is 6 squared plus 2 squared.
Q729.L4t: The square has an area of twenty.
Q729.L2f: The two diagonals of a square are perpendicular but have different lengths.
Q729.L3f: The side of the square runs between the two given points with legs of 3 and 5, so the side squared is the sum of those squares and the area follows directly.
Q729.L4f: The square has an area of thirty-four.
